prompt.context: After many years of 'tough on crime' positions by politicians without regard to government budgetary implications, and the economic and social impact on low income and black and brown communities, popular sentiment has finally shifted and forced Congress to address criminal justice reform in a meaningful way. Our client is the chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee and wants our help getting their initiative passed. This will be an extremely politically sensitive project, and Congressional leadership on both sides have decided to consider rewriting the laws they previously co-sponsored in their decades in office. In order to both ensure their re-election and prevent making waves that would interfere with their campaign contributions, they have decided to 'Ban the Box'. 'Ban the Box' means remove the check box in job applications that asks applicants upfront to declare whether they have a criminal record. This box is often used as a disqualifier which makes it exceedingly difficult for Formerly Incarcerated Persons (FIPs) and those with any justice-involvement to find jobs commensurate with their qualifications. A major part of this bill will be not only the elimination of the checkbox on applications, but also regulating the appropriate use of criminal background checks after a conditional offer is made. Members of Congress on both sides feel that this bill will: 1. Create a more equitable environment for FIPs to re-enter society as well as a fair chance for people with justice involvement; 2. Lower their likelihood of recidivism; and 3. Balance the need for employers to consider relevant factors in their hiring processes.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider when advising the client on a nationwide 'Ban the Box' bill?

clarifying_info.q: Where geographically would the Ban the Box extend?
clarifying_info.a: This bill would cover all American states and territories and all employers (business, government, nonprofit etc.) operating in the US that interacts with the federal government or across state lines (due to limits of federal legislative powers).

clarifying_info.q: What companies would a Ban the Box bill apply to?
clarifying_info.a: Ban the Box would apply to all federal government jobs, companies and employers that contract with the federal government, and employers that operate either interstate or internationally. Our client expects that most states will follow suit with their own statutory laws soon after passage of this bill.

framework: FIPs: number currently released, number projected released over relevant horizon, recidivism rate broken down by geography / race / socioeconomic status
Ban the Box Program: nationwide implementation scope (states with existing programs vs. states likely to follow), structure and design of the bill
Risks: PR risks (media, advocacy groups), effectiveness risks (will it work, unintended consequences)

questions.prompt: What economic and social factors could be used to engender support for this bill among senators on both sides of the aisle? (This is a politically sensitive issue requiring at least 60 Senate votes.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm using a structured approach separating economic from social factors. Strong answers cover multiple distinct buckets rather than listing loosely related ideas.

questions.prompt: What information do you need to calculate how many FIPs would stay out of prison if their employment was 100%? Calculate the number for newly released FIPs over the next 3 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the required data inputs (total incarcerated, release rate, recidivism rate, share of recidivism attributable to unemployment) before calculating. The key evaluative moment is the 'So What': the candidate should contextualize the number and discuss how it can influence policy, and flag the risks of the underlying assumptions.

math.setup: Total incarcerated = 2.4M. 25% released annually => 0.6M per year => 1.8M over 3 years. 70% of FIPs are reincarcerated => ~1.26M returned to incarceration. 20% of recidivism is due to unemployment => 1.26M x 20% = ~252k FIPs stay out of prison if employment is 100%.
math.answer: Approximately 250,000 FIPs would remain out of prison over 3 years if their employment rate were 100%.

questions.prompt: The ranking minority member wants to expand 'Ban the Box' to college applications in exchange for co-sponsorship. What are some positives of expanding Ban the Box to cover college admissions?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm creatively and structure the positives across individual, societal, and economic dimensions. Strong answers reference the broader mission of reducing recidivism and cite concrete mechanisms.

brainstorming.prompt: What economic and social factors could be used to engender support for this bill?

categories.name: Economic Factors
ideas: Increased employment rate among FIPs
More tax revenue from employed FIPs
Fewer people on government assistance programs
Lower recidivism means fewer people incarcerated and major budget savings for prison systems
Signals employers to tap into a broader talent pool that is more loyal and could reduce turnover

categories.name: Social Factors
ideas: Less fear of background checks among FIPs
Higher application rates increasing hope and participation in the workforce
Easier for FIPs to rejoin their communities
Stronger community ties
Redemption — giving people a fair chance after they have served their time
70 million people in the US have a criminal record; politically, many people and their families could be positively impacted

categories.name: College Admissions Extension Positives
ideas: Creates educational opportunities for FIPs; education leads to further opportunities
College degree holders earn more, improving lives of them and their families
Higher incomes mean more taxes paid, contributing more to communities
Gives greater diversity to college classes
Avoids ruining someone's life for a single mistake
Prison sentences serve as paying a debt to society; continued punishment is unnecessary and unfair
Will further lower recidivism (RAND study: college/education behind bars reduced recidivism by 40%)
Further removes social stigma associated with being a FIP
Provides access to career-track jobs rather than only transitional work
Diversity of FIPs can help fill talent gaps for employers in key sectors like tech and healthcare

recommendation: Recommend that the client put forward a bipartisan Ban the Box bill eliminating the criminal record checkbox and regulating or restricting the use of criminal background checks for both employment and college admissions.
risks: Politicians will face strong opposition from lobbyists and companies that profit from the prison industrial complex and may not follow through on their promise to support the bill.
next_steps: Advise the client to begin preparing the bill for passage.
Begin lobbying fellow senators to ensure the necessary votes for approval.
